newsitem.title: JAPAN: Possible burden of railway debt clouds JR earnings.
newsitem.headline: Possible burden of railway debt clouds JR earnings.

text.p: The annual earnings of two firms belonging to the formerly state-run Japan Railways (JR) group may be within expectations, but analysts warned on Monday that a big question mark was looming over their future prospects.
Investors are nervously waiting to see whether the JR firms will yield to growing political pressure to shoulder more of Japan's hefty railway debt, they said.
If the JR firms were forced to share more of the snowballing debt left by the national railway firm, business would be severely damaged and investors would shy away from their shares, analysts said.

On Wednesday West Japan Railway Co (JR West) is due to unveil its first annual earnings report since its listing last October, which will be followed by East Japan Railway Co's (JR East) earnings report on Thursday.

JR West expects a parent current profit of 52 billion yen ($448 million) in the last business year ended March 31, down from an actual 55.62 billion yen ($479 million) in 1995/96. It forecasts a profit of 48 billion yen ($413 million) this year.

JR East sees its parent current profit growing to an estimated 103 billion yen ($887 million) last year, from an actual 102.15 billion yen ($880 million) profit in 1995/96. It forecasts this year's profit at 87 billion yen ($750 million).
Analysts said last year's earnings would probably be in line with forecasts, but said the future outlook was unclear.
Japan's railway debt has swollen to 28.1 trillion yen ($242 billion) from 25.5 trillion yen ($219 billion) in 1987, when the government inherited two-thirds of Japanese National Railways' (JNR) debt.
At that time, the heavily indebted JNR was split into seven JR group companies, which took over one-third of the debt.
The government had hoped to slash the debt by selling land left by JNR and by listing state-owned shares of JR firms, but this has been delayed while interest payments have grown.
Government officials have said the crucial decision on when and how to repay the debt, which is estimated to cost taxpayers 20 trillion yen ($172 billion), must be made in a year or two.
Some legislators have urged the government to force JR firms to bear more of the debt.
Analysts, however, said such a plan would damage the earnings of JR firms, which would be forced to raise train fares and possibly lose competitiveness.
"If JR firms have to shoulder (a larger) part of the debt burden, their earnings would be impacted tremendously," said Naoko Matsumoto, analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.

Matsumoto estimated that a 10 percent increase in the train fares of three major JR companies -- JR East, JR West, and Central Japan Railway Co, known as JR Tokai -- would reduce their combined profits by 36 percent. A 20 percent increase would lead to a 72 percent fall in their profits, she added.
"Besides, overseas investors in particular could turn away from shares of formerly state-owned bodies," she said.

Jun Harada, analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities & Economics, said: "It (an increased debt burden on JR firms) would do little to offset the huge debt, while hurting the firms' competitiveness (in the transportation industry)."
If profitability declines, JR firms would find it difficult to make new share listings, as investor demand would wane and possibly lead to a JR share supply glut, analysts said.
Unless the government swiftly decides how to pay the debt, JR Tokai shares, due to be listed in October, may not attract enthusiastic buying, they said.
The government is also due to sell its remaining 1.5 million shares in JR East, the first company to go public in the JR group, after 2.5 million shares were listed in 1993.
JR firms have already been through a tough period, as they have had to try to reduce costs to prepare for 1997/98, which started in April, when a new tax on fixed assets was introduced.
"The earnings results for 1996/97 will be a touchstone to see whether they will succeed in cutting costs for next year," said Tadatoshi Utaka, analyst at Nikko Research Center.
